deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics: no formulas, computations or derivations. It is a philosophical-psychological fragment, the opening of Riemann's 'Zur Psychologie und Metaphysik' (part of the 'Fragmente philosophischen Inhalts', Naturphilosophie). Dedekind and Weber printed this fragment in the Gesammelte Werke (1876; 2nd ed. 1892). I am recalling that edition, not comparing against it here. The argument runs as follows.

(a) Every simple act of thought ('einfacher Denkact') deposits something permanent and substantial in the soul.

(b) This substance appears as a unity. But insofar as it expresses something extended in space and time, it seems to contain an inner manifold. Riemann therefore names it 'Geistesmasse' (mind-mass).

(c) Geistesmassen entering the soul appear to us as Vorstellungen (representations). The differing qualities of representations are conditioned by the differing (inner) form of the Geistesmassen, that is, by differences in the process by which they are formed.

(d) Newly forming Geistesmassen combine to a definite degree, partly with one another and partly with older ones. Their 'entry' into the soul simply consists in this combination with the older Geistesmassen.

(e) Hence the soul is a compact Geistesmasse, connected within itself in the closest and most manifold ways. It grows continually through newly entering Geistesmassen, and its development ('Fortbildung') rests on this.

(f) Numbered theses follow:
- 4) Geistesmassen once formed are imperishable and their connections indissoluble. Only the relative strength of the connections changes as new Geistesmassen are added.
- 5) The persistence of Geistesmassen and their connections needs no material substrate, and they exert no lasting effect on the phenomenal world. Hence they bear no relation to any part of matter and have no seat in space.
- 6) By contrast, all formation and connection of new Geistesmassen requires a material carrier. Hence all thinking happens at a definite place.

(g) A parenthetical empirical support: according to experience, only thinking is effortful, and the expenditure of force is, as far as we can estimate, proportional to mental activity. In modern terms this is a heuristic claim that energetic cost scales with mental activity, offered as evidence that thought formation is physically located. The text gives no formula.

Context: Riemann (influenced by Herbart) is building a speculative 'mechanics of the mind' that parallels his ether/field speculations in the Naturphilosophie fragments. The term 'Mannigfaltigkeit' appears here in a non-technical sense, echoing his habilitation vocabulary. The numbering starts at 4), which suggests that the preceding unnumbered paragraphs implicitly serve as points 1)-3).

No implicit mathematical steps exist to fill in.
errors: Philosophically, thesis 5 (persistence without material substrate, no seat in space) sits in tension with thesis 6 (formation requires a material carrier at a definite place). Riemann deliberately separates formation from persistence; this is a metaphysical position, not a logical error.
The proportionality of 'Kraftaufwand' to mental activity is asserted only qualitatively ('so weit wir das schätzen können'). It is not quantified or justified.

results.what: Doctrine of 'Geistesmassen': permanent mental substances deposited by acts of thought, whose combination constitutes the soul; formation is localized and material, persistence is non-spatial.
results.modern_name: Speculative psychology/metaphysics in the Herbartian tradition (associationist theory of representations); cf. later 'memory trace'/engram ideas
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann himself (published posthumously in Gesammelte Werke, 1876); background J. F. Herbart's Psychologie als Wissenschaft (1824-25), G. T. Fechner

results.what: Claim that the energetic cost of thinking is proportional to mental activity, used to argue that thinking occurs at a definite place.
results.usually_credited_to: General 19th-century psychophysics (Fechner, Helmholtz era); this text is Riemann's published fragment

deep.surprise_reason: This is the well-known opening of Riemann's philosophical fragment 'Zur Psychologie und Metaphysik', published by Dedekind and Weber in the Gesammelte Werke (1876) and frequently discussed by historians, e.g. in connection with Herbart. It contains no mathematics and nothing unpublished of substance.
transcription_corrections: The superscript word above 'Form' (transcribed '{+innere[?]+}') is uncertain in the image. It may read 'geistige' rather than 'innere'; the printed edition should be consulted.
'Die [-in-] sich bildenden': a short struck-out word precedes 'sich bildenden'. The intended reading is 'Die sich bildenden Geistesmassen'.

'Ihr Eintreten[?] in die Seele besteht[?] in ihrer Verbindung mit den [-ihr-] [-vorhandenen-] älteren Geistesmassen': both readings marked [?] are confirmed by context. The struck words are deletions, so the text reads 'mit den älteren Geistesmassen'.
'Nach den Ergebnissen[?] unserer Erfahrungen' is uncertain. The word after 'Nach' may be read differently (e.g. 'dem Verhalten'); treat it as unverified.

The pencil marginal note beside thesis 6 (transcribed 'Jeder Act eigentl[?] Seelenleben[?]') is in a different hand and medium, probably a later annotation; the reading is uncertain (possibly 'Jeder Act eines Seelenlebens'). Also, a pencil '143' at the upper right edge differs from the circled folio number '140'.
